utterances.text: When Milan Babic rejected the Vance Plan and when the political preconditions were met for various districts within Croatia to unite, it was necessary for somebody to accept to become the president of the Serbian Krajina. It never crossed my mind before that it should be me, but Milan Paspalj, president of the assembly, and some more of my associates of mine, talked me into it, saying that it would be a temporary solution, that the situation requires it, that it can be only me because I am able to reconcile all the different parties, and that I am the only acceptable solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you accepted - and, if so, to what extent - in the part of the Serbian Krajina that was called the Knin Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the people in that part of Krajina, I was not really known. I was perhaps known to the SDS leadership, but the people didn't know me, and the elections later showed that I was never very well accepted there. When I say "elections," I mean those in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering that the Republic of Serbian Krajina was made up of three then separate units, can you tell us to what extent their political and other interests coincided? Did they enable them to form one integral whole and carry on with the harmonised policy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I've spoken about this here before, whether I'll be repeating myself, the interests of Serbs from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem were not really such that they would justify unification with Serbs who were 600 kilometres away from us in the Knin Krajina. We saw it as a temporary and a formal arrangement because the recognition of former Yugoslav republics was on the agenda at the time, and we thought that those republics that had been formed within what we called Communist borders do not have real statehood, or basis, for recognition so that if they are recognised, the Serbian Krajina could also be recognised because it had a basis in history within the former Austro-Hungarian empire, they were recognised before as the so-called military Krajina. That's why I accepted this post in its temporary and formal dimension. Later on, it assumed a very serious practical dimension as well, where all the resources from Eastern Slavonia were appropriated by the western parts for the whole thing later to escalate and the military personnel from Eastern Slavonia later had to be mobilised to defend Western Slavonia, and that was intolerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have seen and you probably know the constitution of the Republic of Serbian Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L3. It is tab 1178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the document number for the record, please, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The document number is L3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to page 7, Article 78. In English, it's page 23. We can move to the previous page, just to see who is responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Under the constitution that was in force at the time when you were elected, you had certain responsibilities. And let us now look at point 5 of this article. It's on the next page. Paragraph 5: Controls armed forces in peace and in war and people's resistance in wartime, you order general and partial mobilisation, organise preparations for defence, et cetera. How did you understand this particular responsibility?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer your specific question, I should only like to say that this constitution of 19 December, 1991, was adopted when Milan Babic was president and, in gest, my friends and I called it Babic's constitution. And in this part that relates to the responsibilities of the president, only Babic's picture was missing. In my own exercise of the duties of president, I did not want the duties and powers of the president of the republic to be so great. As for your question, especially as far as military aspects are concerned, I understood my position as president of the republic in a very realistic way, in the sense that I was aware of my lack of knowledge and experience. And when you read this point "controls armed forces," to me, it meant a political function because command required professional skills, and I didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at Article 102 of the constitution. It is on page 9 of the original and page 31 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were elected to the post of the president of the republic, I see that the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina were made only of the Territorial Defence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. The Territorial Defence had already been established before I came to this position. I think that it was established in accordance with the federal law and that General Torbica was in charge of it, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember whether at the time when you were elected the JNA was still present in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. The JNA was present up until the end of May or early June. It was there parallelly. When I say "parallelly," I mean that it was completely independent from the organs of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P2637. It is tab 597.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could please look at the screen, do you see this order on organisational and establishment changes in the units of the Republic of Serbian Krajina Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move one page forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see who adopted this order and when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see, as everyone present, that it was issued by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence on the 27th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Under A, under Roman numeral I, the setting up of staffs and units of Territorial Defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina is ordered, the time needed for mobilisation, and so on. If we go through the document, we will see that other units and staffs of Territorial Defence are being formed as well. What I'm interested in is whether you participated in any way in the drawing up of this order. Did you play any role in this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not play any role, and I did not take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And was such an order submitted to you as the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, though you had been elected just a day before. But did you ever receive it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that some organisational changes were underway, that some staffs and units were being set up, and so on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. Because I only came to Knin later. Perhaps it was in March. I don't remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see please 1D3563. It is tab 1416.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you can see the materials from the Federal Secretariat of the Interior dated the 24th of February, 1992, sent to the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. It says here that basics of the organisation of the internal affairs service in the Republic of Serbian Krajina are hereby submitted. And also an outline of the proposed organisation of the internal affairs service and the Law on Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Though you had not yet been elected at the time, did you know that something like this was being prepared; that is to say, that the Federal Secretariat of the Interior was preparing these materials and the future organisation of internal affairs in the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you later informed about this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw it first here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you later possibly participate in any way whatsoever or were informed about the preparation of the Law on Internal Affairs, or did you know that the organs of the interior were being organised?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection. The witness has not laid a sufficient foundation. He doesn't know anything about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll not -- I withdraw my request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your term in office, were the armed forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina ever used, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several times. If I remember well, the first occasion was at Miljevacki Plateau, then there was the Croatian action Maslenica, and in September 1993, theMedak pocket. So these were the major uses when we were more fiercely attacked. And there were many other individual instances of lesser intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you, by any chance, remember when this action at the Miljevacki Plateau took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that was in June 1992, as soon as the UN took over the zone of responsibility from the JNA and the JNA withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- or, rather, can you tell us anything about an action that was carried out in the corridor. This was not in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina but in another territory. But if you could tell us what was happening and when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian forces cut through the corridor which linked us with the eastern and western parts in the area of Brcko. Some of the forces of the Republic of Serbian Krajina then participated in breaking through the corridor, together with the forces of RepublikaSrpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the importance of this corridor for the Republic of Serbian Krajina or at least for the former SAO Krajina or the Knin Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was vitally important, essentially important, not just for the former SAO Krajina but all of Bosnian Krajina as well, the whole area that included Banja Luka, Doboj, and so on, because otherwise we would have been cut off, as if you cut off the root of the plant. Including Banja Luka and Doboj, not Dobrinja, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the threat? What could not take place if the corridor was cut off?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most simply put, any sort of communication had been cut off, so the movement of people and goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in spring 1992. I don't know if it was May or not. I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us, was that after the JNA had withdrawn or before it withdrew, while the JNA was still there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a generally known fact. I could have checked up, but I think it may have been around this time, but I can't say whether it was before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember whether the JNA units participated in the liberation of the corridor, or was it just the troops you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well that the JNA units did not participate. It was the forces of the RSK and the forces of RepublikaSrpska which took part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time you had frequent contacts with international representatives. Let me not show you any documents. I don't think it is necessary because I suppose that you remember that one of their requests, one that was often voiced, was that all Territorial Defence units and even the police should be disarmed. How did you perceive this request and how did everyone perceive that, especially in the context of the attacks on the corridor that you just talked about and also the attack on the Miljevac Plateau?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed the problem with Mr. Goulding and Mr. Vance when the Vance Plan was being adopted. For us, for me, for the leadership and for most of the people, it was not logical to disarm only one side while leaving the other side practically with full combat equipment on the other side of the line of demarcation. And the mediators primarily guaranteed that the United Nations forces would be able to provide security for us. However, once it was agreed and the United Nations did come, it turned out that this was not possible. And I think that that position was not a fair one: To disarm one side while allowing the other side to attack wherever and whenever they wanted, without any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of those demands, what was your own position in relation to those demands during the talks?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, I believed those people who provided those guarantees, but as time went by, I became more and more skeptical and began to lose faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the position of other organs of authority in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina; for example, of the government, the Territorial Defence, and the people also who lived there, in relation to these demands?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most of them were a bit more hard-line than I was. I was a bit more naive and more trusting. But because of the bad experiences that we had had in World War II and in general, there was a lot of fear among the people. They didn't have a lot of confidence in what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And who was it that they were not confident about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they did not trust that the Croatian side would respect the agreement. All the weapons were left with the Croats. They were just a couple of kilometres away from the -- their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us anything about the position -- well, we can see that by law and by constitution, you were in charge of the armed forces. So what was your practical position throughout the entire period, not only when you were elected in 1992 but throughout your term of office as the president of the Serbian Republic of the Krajina till 1993? What was your position regarding the armed forces, because this changed so it was not just the TO that was making them up?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was aware that I didn't have any military training and that I was only in charge in the formal extent, whereas, all the other decision-making was entrusted to the people who were capable of making such decisions. Everything that I signed and all the decisions that I made were a result of things that were proposed by those people. None of that was something that came from me. Basically I was just carrying out the formal aspect of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L49. It is tab 1214. We can move on next page of English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In April 1993, the constitution was amended, the constitution of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, when it was declared that the Republic of the Serbian Krajina had an army, that it had its permanent and reserve forces. First of all, are you able to tell us whether this establishment of the Army of the Serbian Krajina in April 1993 had anything to do with earlier events in the military area, anything to do with confrontations that occurred in the area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believed that this was a forced move, that we had to do this, because there were constant threats and attacks coming from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular event that preceded this amendment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already referred to it. It was the so-called Maslenica action in January of 1992. Sorry, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the amendment was made, was there an attempt made to reach a peaceful solution, to achieve a peaceful withdrawal from the territory in question, or was this measure immediately resorted to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we did not immediately resort to this measure. We tried everything to find a peaceful solution. I took part in negotiations to implement an UN resolution requesting Croatia to return to its pre-aggression positions. The talks were conducted in New York on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't come to much. If we keep in mind that Croatia did not implement the resolution, they didn't withdraw, and they didn't accept anything. UN troops did not protect us either. I even had information that they actually were helping the Croatian side with some intelligence matters. More specifically, it was the French Battalion. I had the opportunity this year in a TV programme on Croatian television to hear this from one of the commanders of their units in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Amendment 12 also states that the commander of the Army of RepublikaSrpska Krajina is appointed by the assembly upon the proposal of the Supreme Defence Council. Do you know who was appointed commander of the Serbian Army of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was Mile Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next amendment, Amendment 13 - it's on the next page of the English translation - changes your powers, the powers of the president of the republic. Now it says that you are at the head of the Army of the Serbian Krajina pursuant to the constitution and decisions of the Supreme Defence Council and that you preside over the Supreme Defence Council. Are you able to tell us how you understood this role of presiding over the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood it for what it was; that is, that I was first among equals, everybody was there on an equal footing, and I was just the person who was chairing the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us who were other members of this body, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also the commander of the army. There were three government members: The prime minister, the defence minister, and the minister of the interior. And, of course, I, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to make a comparison between your own knowledge of military affairs and the knowledge of military affairs of any other member of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prime minister and I were in an inferior position in such terms in relation to the other three. The commander of the army and the defence minister were the most knowledgeable among us in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Amendment 13 also states that you were also authorised to make decisions on the setting up, the seat, and the competence of military courts and prosecutor's offices and to appoint and dismiss the president and judges of the military court and prosecutor's office. Are you able to tell us if this decision was actually implemented during your term of office? Were military courts and prosecutor's offices actually set up from April 1993 until the end of the year? I'm talking about that period.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really be sure about that now, so I cannot state that with any degree of certainty. However, I understood this constitutional amendment in general terms, because I didn't have an expert team in the president's office, so I would have had to sign the formal decision based on recommendations of a government expert team.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at Amendment 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm only going to ask you about the powers of the Supreme Defence Council. I can see that, amongst other things, the Supreme Defence Council was in charge of declaring the possibility of an imminent threat of war and dealt with mobilisation. Could you please tell me whether this was actually part of your powers originally as president of the republic before these an amendments were made?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember after the Maslenica action by Croatian forces you did declare a state of war and -- and mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was your position towards the government of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina? What were your powers in relation to that body?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to put it in the clearest terms, I thought that they were like a parallel body. I and the government were responsible to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "parallel body," you mean to the extent that you were elected by the assembly and were responsible to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never saw the government as a body that was under me, controlled by me, a body on which I could impose my own will.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were your powers separated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the constitution has dealt with that. They were separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the government submit to you any reports, like work progress reports, what measures it should take? Did they consult you on the steps to be taken?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it never did. In fact, I don't remember that the government ever consulted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L54.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain to us Article 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in a bit? I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to clear this up considering that it is written in the constitution that the president controls armed forces and that the army is commanded by the commander of the Serbian Army of Krajina. And here in the law, we see that the army is under the command of the president of the republic. Is it because the law was passed a few days before the amendments?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously. Because, otherwise, the law would be anti-constitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to the first page just to see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My impression is that this law was passed before those amendments that were enacted on the 22nd, that is, two days later. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection to the leading question about what counsel's impression is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me on what date the Law on the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was passed.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can all see, it was on 20th April, 1993. That's two days before those amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see the next page of this document in original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see Article 6 which reads: "The army commander shall command the army in keeping with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council."

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this provision enforced during the rest of your term of office, that the army commander commands the Army of the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only way it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever command the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, and I wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L55. It is tab 1218.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 8th amendment, enacted in May 1992, which stipulates that the president of the republic shall appoint the commander of the Territorial Defence and also assess judges, or judge/jurors. The powers that the president here -- are phrased in such a way that the president appoints the TO commander but is not able to dismiss him.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he can only appoint and dismiss presidents of courts, but not the TO commander. He cannot dismiss the TO commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were elected president of the RSK, who was the commander of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Army of Krajina -- sorry, Territorial Defence. And who appointed him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the commander was General Milan Torbica, and I believe he was appointed by the federal secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that, in accordance with this provision, you were not able to replace him or to dismiss him from that position, if you saw fit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's obvious from this amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, L8. It is tab 1183.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision on the return of refugees. In the original, it's on the left. You are probably familiar with this decision. It was discussed also during the examination-in-chief. What can you tell us about this decision? Do you know when it was passed? Was it the subject of debate? Or discussion with representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it was passed on the 21st of April, 1992. I don't know specifically whether it was discussed with representatives of the international community, considering that it's a decision of the government. But I know we discussed with the international community the general issue of the return of refugees, and I suppose that this decision isin line with those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, speaking of the return of refugees, which refugees did you discuss with the international representatives?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our side wanted those discussions to cover Serb refugees as well, but representatives of the international community were only interested in Croat refugees. They were not interested in Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did a problem occur about the return of Croat refugees; and, if so, what was the problem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was more than one problem, but the main one was that those Croat houses were now occupied by Serb refugees, and we had to find some way to provide accommodation. There were no specific proposals. There was just the demand for Croats to return, and I had a feeling that Serb refugees were second-class citizens. Nobody even mentioned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did negotiators offer some mediation with the Croat authorities to enable Serb refugees to return to their homes at the same time as the Croats would return to theirs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our first and principal demand, but we did not meet with any understanding. The negotiators did try, but they were not very firm in their attempts, whereas, Croatia did not even want to discuss it. But there were more problems. Croat refugees did not want to return into an area that was under our authority. So, at the time, it was practically impossible to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I would need a few minutes for administrative matters. So if it is convenient for you to do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. First thing is the private or public session and lifting eventually some parts of the private designation we gave yesterday. You've probably seen Mr. Stringer's suggestions in this regard. Do you have a position on them or would you need to look into them further?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I -- I'd like to have some -- some time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We hear from you; right? Then how long -- how long would you still have with this witness, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- I don't know at the moment how much time I have, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Some time ago you -- pardon? Three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do my best to finish tomorrow, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- maybe some time would be needed, additional time would be needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hadzic, we'll adjourn for the day. You're still a witness under oath. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of July, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
